1:
Two names stand in the heading and only one family follows it, and every witness feels the oddity. Gill takes the order to be simple seniority — Aaron is named first because he is the elder — and observes that the descendants of the one were priests while those of the other were merely Levites, so obscure that they are not named at all but swallowed up among the Amramites. Wesley says the same and draws the reason tighter: Moses' children are mentioned so obscurely because they were common Levites, the priesthood having been given solely to Aaron's posterity, and that is why Aaron here precedes the brother who elsewhere precedes him. Ellicott adds the structural point. Moses' ministry was restricted to his own person and his sons are simply classed among the Levitical families elsewhere, whereas Aaron's office was perpetuated in his descendants; alternatively both men were made heads of the whole tribe, so that the Levitical families generally are traced up to the two of them equally. Keil and Delitzsch read the heading as doing deliberate work at the outset — fixing the position the Levites will occupy relative to the priests before a single name is counted — and take the generations to be the Levitical families named after Moses and Aaron as their spiritual fathers, which makes the note of time no idle repetition.

Clarke is willing to doubt the text. Since only Aaron's family appears, some have thought the name of Moses was not originally there; others resolve it by rendering the word not generations but acts or transactions, the history rather than the descent. What he does with the silence is the striking thing. Moses passed by his own family, gave them no rank or privilege while he lived and left them nothing when he died, and they were absorbed into the Levites without distinction — which Clarke takes for evidence of where the religion came from. Had it been a man's invention it must have had some impure passion for its object, lust or ambition or avarice; none appears in the whole of an administration in which he had it constantly in his power to gratify each.

The two who died are recalled without being re-narrated. Calvin notes that Moses only touches briefly here on what he had told at length, that of four sons two survived their father, Nadab and Abihu having paid the penalty of their negligence. Henry makes the recital a preamble deliberately placed: the example stands at the head of the law of the priesthood as a warning to all succeeding priests that God is a jealous God, and that the holy anointing oil was an honour to the obedient but no shelter to the disobedient. Their childlessness he reads as part of the punishment, so that none of their line should remain to bear up the name they had profaned. And he hears something in the phrase that describes the survivors, who ministered in the sight of Aaron: they kept under their father's eye and took instruction from him, whereas Nadab and Abihu had probably got out of his sight when they offered the strange fire. Wesley fixes the chronology that the heading assumes — at Sinai those two were still alive, though dead by the time this account was taken.
5:
Calvin finds two heads in the paragraph: that the Levites were set apart for the sanctuary, and that they were to do nothing except by the authority of Aaron's house. On the first he presses that the choice was gratuitous, so that nobody might suppose himself worthy of so honourable a charge; and he draws from it a lesson about the whole congregation, since if the Levites had not stood between, the law shut the rest of the people out from access to God. On the second he goes further than the text obliges him to. The exalting of one priest over all the others was meant to direct them to the one Mediator, and the supreme power of Christ was represented in Aaron — from which he turns on those who wrest the arrangement into an argument for setting bishops over presbyters and so, by stages, for the primacy of Rome. Ministers are placed under the hand of Christ to usurp no dominion but to render account to the Prince of pastors, and a distinction of ranks that has order for its object is not to be repudiated, provided it neither obscures Christ's glory nor serves ambition. He ends where the argument began, that no man takes this honour on himself.

The verb of presenting is read as a sacrificial one. Clarke says the original is properly the word for bringing an offering, so that the tribe was given up entirely, no longer its own but the Lord's property; Wesley renders it simply as offering them to the Lord for special service, promised before and now actually conferred. Keil and Delitzsch prefer the servant's posture, the ordinary expression for standing before a master to receive his commands.

What the Levites were to keep is disputed in a small way with large consequences. Ellicott sets out two possibilities: the word may mean the directions the Levites were to receive from Aaron, or — and he thinks this likelier, since the same word is used in the next breath of the congregation — the charge laid upon Aaron and the whole congregation in the matter of public worship. Wesley takes it the second way and spells out the substitution: the sacrifices and services due from all the people could not be performed by the people in their own persons, so they were performed by particular persons in their stead, formerly by the firstborn and now by these. Gill puts the same duty defensively, as securing the sanctuary from being polluted or plundered and easing both the priests and the people. Keil and Delitzsch keep it concrete — the oversight of the furniture, to keep it safe and clean.

Two witnesses stop at a repeated word. Both Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch note that given is doubled for emphasis, expressing complete surrender, and both are careful to separate these given ones from the later temple servants of foreign descent who were assigned to the Levites as slaves for the lowest duties (Joshua 9:27). Ellicott adds why this tribe and no other was available for the honour: they had shown themselves the most zealous for the Lord at the golden calf, and it was then that Moses charged them to fill their hands. Wesley closes the paragraph by defining the intruder as widely as the law does — every man not of Aaron's family, though he be a Levite.
11:
The reason for the whole arrangement is now given, and it reaches back to Egypt. Keil and Delitzsch trace the chain: when God slew the firstborn of Egypt he sanctified to himself all the firstborn of Israel, of man and beast; the nation, itself adopted as his firstborn son, was therefore bound to dedicate its firstborn sons to the sanctuary; and now the Levites and their cattle are adopted in their place and the firstborn released. What is gained by it, they add, is not merely a substitution but a better order of service, since one tribe would devote itself to this vocation undividedly where the firstborn of all the tribes could not. Calvin puts the same title in terms of purchase. Those whose lives were gratuitously spared in the general slaughter were bought for God, and having the free option of claiming the firstborn of every tribe he was equally at liberty to take a twelfth part of the people from one — which, he says, cuts off all handle for complaint, since it would have been intolerable ingratitude to withdraw from his control men he had miraculously redeemed. Gill states the sovereignty barely: it was his own act and deed, done of his own will and pleasure, and none should contradict him.

Why Levi in particular is a question two of the witnesses canvass and neither settles by one reason alone. Clarke reviews the answers and finds them inconclusive. The zeal of the tribe in cutting down the worshippers of the calf has been thought sufficient, but he prefers a plainer consideration — that this was the smallest tribe and quite enough for the service, a more numerous tribe being at that time very inconvenient. Wesley gathers three reasons together rather than choosing: partly God's respect to Moses and Aaron, who were of it; partly a recompence of the tribe's zeal against idolaters; and partly that it was the smallest, and therefore most likely to find both employment in the work and maintenance from it.

Wesley also asks the question the exchange raises about the men displaced. The firstborn had been God's property, and the administration of holy things was formerly committed to them; that is now taken away, either because they forfeited it by joining their brethren in the calf, or because they were to be occupied with the distribution of the inheritances they were going in to possess and could not be at leisure. He adds the reason for concentrating the office in a single tribe instead of leaving some men in each: scattered custodians might have become an occasion of idolatry, confusion, division and contempt of sacred things.

Ellicott raises a difficulty in the older command that this one presupposes. The direction to sanctify the firstborn stands immediately after the exodus and the institution of the Passover, and its terms do not make clear whether it applied to the firstborn then living — which he thinks by far the more probable — or was simply prospective. He notes that the whole nation is called the Lord's firstborn son (Exodus 4:22), so that the firstborn sons appear to stand as representatives of the entire people. Clarke, following Ainsworth, carries the type forward instead of back, to a congregation of the firstborn whose names are written in heaven.
14:
One rule governs this muster and it is not the rule used for the other tribes. Henry states the contrast plainly: the rest were numbered from twenty years old and upward, and of those only such as could go out to war, whereas here infants and infirm alike are taken in, the tribe being exempt from war. He knows how few of them the service actually needed — little more than a third, some eight thousand of twenty-two — and makes the surplus the point. God would have them all numbered as retainers of his family, so that none should think himself disowned merely because he was not in a capacity to serve; a Levite of a month old could not honour God as the grown could, and yet out of the mouths of babes the praise of the tribe was perfected. He adds the descent rule, that they were reckoned after the house of their fathers and not their mothers, since the son of a Levite's daughter who married outside the tribe was no Levite. He also looks ahead to the total and to the three hundred by which the families overshoot it, supposing that those struck off the account were the firstborn of the Levites themselves, born since the coming out of Egypt and already sanctified, so that they could not enter the exchange; had they been counted in, the balance would have fallen the other way. Set beside the other tribes, he observes, Levi was by much the smallest of them all, God's part in the world being often the smallest part.

The others explain the month-old rule by the exchange it serves. Clarke argues from arithmetic: numbered from twenty they would not have come near the firstborn of the twelve tribes, and since those firstborn were of all ages their substitutes had to be of all ages too. Ellicott notes the same age governs the firstborn themselves and was afterwards fixed as the age of redemption (Numbers 18:16). Wesley gives the reason from the other end — a month was when the firstborn were offered — and points out that for other purposes the Levites are numbered from twenty-five and from thirty, as they entered part and then the whole of their work. Calvin makes the counting of infants an act of fairness: had God taken only those past twenty it could not have been known how many firstborn there were and the compensation would have been uncertain, so the indulgence should have made the people readier to pay for the shortfall, and it would have been an act of malignity to refuse him what he asked after he had condescended to so just a compact.

Clarke notices who did the counting, and finds a delicacy in it. Moses and Aaron together numbered the twelve tribes, but Moses numbered the Levites alone; and since the money redeeming the surplus firstborn was to be paid to Aaron and his sons, it was decent that the man whose advantage it was that the firstborn should exceed the Levites should not be the one authorised to take that number himself. Gill notes only that the tribe was left out of the general muster and counted apart, differently and for a different purpose.

The three names that open the families draw one reflection from Calvin. Levi begot three sons, of whom two had two sons each and one had four; that twelve men should have grown in so short a time into so many thousands is a thing nobody would have expected, and it shows how powerfully God works under the semblance of weakness. That Kohath's house was promoted above the rest he refers to the same gratuitous good pleasure that called Moses — adding that lest Moses be suspected of ambition, God chose that his own sons should remain in the ordinary station of Levites.
21:
The first of the three houses is set out in the fixed order the chapter will keep for all of them: the families that composed it, their number, their station, their chief, and their charge. Gill identifies the two families as the Libnites and the Shimites, from the first son of Levi, and glosses the chief as the man having authority over them and the direction of what they were to do. Keil and Delitzsch give the tally at seven thousand five hundred males and place them under Eliasaph behind the dwelling, on the western side. Ellicott takes the occasion to lay out the whole encampment at once, since the positions of the twelve tribes had already been fixed and these verses fix the positions of the priests and Levites within them: Moses and Aaron with Aaron's sons on the east, the Kohathites south, the Gershonites west, the Merarites north.

Clarke stops at the number and doubts it. He suggests the figure may originally have read two hundred rather than five hundred, the two Hebrew letters being easily confounded — a conjecture he makes here in passing and returns to when the totals fail to agree.

What this house carried is where Ellicott does his closest work, and it turns on a distinction the English blurs. The tent and the tabernacle are not the same thing: the second is the building of shittim wood with its curtains, and the first is the covering over it, so that when the word for tent appears the second time in this verse it means the outer covering of goats' hair. The covering proper he takes to include both the rams' skins and the skins beneath them. The hanging at the entrance was of blue and purple and scarlet and fine twined linen; and the word rendered door means an opening rather than a door, though at a later period, when the tabernacle stood at Shiloh, it did have doors. On the cords he corrects the natural reading: the possessives do not refer to the court, whose cords belonged to the Merarites, but to the dwelling itself — or else each of them refers to everything just mentioned, the phrase meaning whatever had to be done in connection with these things.

Wesley reaches the same allocation in a quarter of the space and by simple exclusion. The tabernacle here does not mean the boards, which belonged to Merari, but the ten curtains; the tent means the curtains of goats' hair; the coverings mean the rams' skins and the skins above them; and the cords are those by which the whole was fastened to the pins and stretched out. Between them the two witnesses divide the fabric of the sanctuary from its frame, and give this house everything that hung and nothing that stood.
27:
The second house is the largest and the most favoured, and the witnesses agree that the favour follows from one fact. Gill notes that the Amramites take their name from the first son of Kohath, the father of Aaron and Moses, so that both men and their children fall inside this family. Ellicott draws the consequence: it was in virtue of that descent that the Kohathites received the most honourable portion of the service, and that Eleazar, Aaron's eldest surviving son, was set over the whole body of the Levites. Keil and Delitzsch describe his office by the word used for it, an oversight or superiority over the chiefs of the three families and over the servants of the sanctuary. Wesley makes the rank precise — next under the high priest, whence he is elsewhere called the second priest, and in the high priest's absence through sickness or other necessity he was to perform his work.

Gill weighs the numbers before he accepts the compliment. Eight thousand six hundred was the largest of the three houses, but since this house had twice as many families as either of the others, the increase was not so large in proportion — the two Gershonite families falling only eleven hundred short of these four. On the station he is equally exact: the south is the right hand and so the more honourable side, the east being reserved for Moses and Aaron; and Ellicott supplies the philology, since the Hebrew name for the south is taken from the word for the right hand, a man facing east having the south on his right. Wesley lists the privileges of the house together — Moses and Aaron and all the priests out of it, the chief place, the care of the most holy things, and twenty-three cities in Canaan, almost as many as both their brethren received — and then repeats the point the chapter keeps making, that the posterity of Moses were not distinguished from other Levites at all.

Their charge was the furniture rather than the fabric. Keil and Delitzsch list it as the ark, the table, the candlestick, the altars and the vessels of the sanctuary, together with the hanging; Wesley identifies that hanging as the one covering the most holy place, all other hangings belonging to the Gershonites.

Gill alone reads the encampment forward into what happens later in the book, and it is the sharpest observation in the section. Because this house pitched on the south, between the tabernacle and the camp of Reuben, Korah, who was a Kohathite, came to be intimately acquainted with Dathan and Abiram, who were Reubenites — which is how a conspiracy came to be made of men from two different tribes. He adds a second motive from the chief named here. Elizaphan was the same man who carried Nadab and Abihu out of the camp and buried them, and he descended from the youngest of the four Kohathite families; some have thought Korah's dissatisfaction began there, at seeing one of a younger house preferred before him.
33:
The third house is the smallest and carries the heaviest load. Gill names the two families from Merari's own sons, and Keil and Delitzsch set the tally at six thousand two hundred males under Zuriel on the northern side. Their charge is the frame of the sanctuary rather than its fabric or its furniture: the boards, the bars, the pillars and the sockets of the dwelling, with all its vessels and everything belonging to its service, and the pillars of the court round about with their sockets, their pins and their cords. Keil and Delitzsch describe the duty as a cycle rather than a custody — to take these things in charge when the dwelling was taken down, to carry them on the march, and to fix them again when it was set up.

Gill explains why this house alone needed help to do it. The boards were the walls of the holy and the most holy place, covered over by the curtains; and because they and what went with them made a heavy carriage, the Merarites were allowed waggons, and were given more of them than the Gershonites, while the Kohathites had none at all. The logic of the whole distribution appears in that one detail: the house that carried cloth needed fewer waggons than the house that carried timber, and the house that carried the ark was to have none, because what it carried was to go on men's shoulders.

One phrase Gill will not take as it stands. Where the text speaks of the chief of the house of the father of the families of Merari, he thinks it should rather be rendered as the chief of the house, the father to the families of Merari — the common father of them all, having the chief authority and power over them — and he notes the same construction elsewhere. The difference is small in English and considerable in sense: on his reading the title does not trace the man's descent but states his office, so that the chief of each house stands to its families as a father rather than merely descending from one.

Ellicott adds nothing here but a cross-reference to the description of the court and its pillars given in Exodus, which is itself a comment of a kind. The three houses have now been set out in the same five slots — family, number, station, chief, charge — and by the third the witnesses have little left to say that they have not already said twice, so that what remains is the pointing of readers back to the place where the objects themselves were described. What the chapter has done in these three paragraphs is to divide one building three ways, and to fix each division to a side of the camp, a named man, and a list of things that could be checked when they were set down.
38:
The fourth side of the square is filled by the priests themselves, and the eastern station is not accidental. Gill notes simply that the entrance into the tabernacle was there, so that Moses and Aaron and Aaron's sons lay across the way in. Ellicott examines the word used for what they kept. The term rendered sanctuary is of wider compass than either the word for the wooden dwelling or the word for the tent that covered it, and appears to take in the court that surrounded it as well; and the charge they kept was, in his gloss, everything that had been commanded to the children of Israel. Wesley offers two readings of the same phrase and declines to choose between them: either the priests kept that charge in the people's stead, which the people were themselves obliged to keep, or they kept it for the people's benefit and preservation.

Then the totals are given, and they do not add up. Keil and Delitzsch state the problem without softening it: the seven thousand five hundred, eight thousand six hundred and six thousand two hundred of the three houses come to twenty-two thousand three hundred, while the muster is recorded as twenty-two thousand. The larger figure cannot be the mistaken one, because the whole later transaction depends on it — the firstborn are said to exceed the Levites by exactly two hundred and seventy-three, which holds only if the Levites were twenty-two thousand.

Two solutions are on offer and they are of the same shape. Keil and Delitzsch first consider the traditional reconciliation, which supposes the three hundred surplus were themselves firstborn Levites who could not be brought into the exchange, and reject it as forced and unsatisfactory, on the ground that the account here is so circumstantial that a fact of that kind would never have been left out of it. Their own proposal is a copyist's error in one of the three family numbers, and they name the likeliest place — the Kohathite figure, where two similar Hebrew words would give eight thousand three hundred rather than eight thousand six hundred. Clarke had already made the same kind of conjecture at the other end of the list, suspecting that the Gershonite seven thousand five hundred should read seven thousand two hundred, two Hebrew letters being easily confounded.

What survives either conjecture is that the recorded total is the sound one, and that the discrepancy sits in a family figure rather than in the sum the rest of the chapter is built on.
40:
The other side of the exchange is now counted. Keil and Delitzsch set out the mechanics: the firstborn of all the tribes from a month old came to twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three, of whom twenty-two thousand were exchanged for the Levites, while the cattle of the Levites were set against the firstlings of the tribes without being numbered or matched head for head. Henry states the rule of the count and reports a stricter version of it — bishop Patrick was decidedly of opinion that none were numbered but those born since the coming out of Egypt, when the firstborn were first sanctified.

Henry then follows that reading where it leads, and it takes him somewhere unexpected. If there were twenty-two thousand firstborn males and as many females, and all of them brought forth in the single year after the exodus, then in the last and bitterest year of the servitude there must have been an abundance of marriages among the Israelites — who were not discouraged by the present distress but married in faith, expecting that their children, though born in bondage, would live in liberty. That the two numbers should come out so near each other he takes for a mark of providence rather than coincidence, since the works of God are known to him beforehand and there is an exact proportion between them.

Ellicott finds the same number a serious difficulty rather than a comfort. Against a male population of some six hundred thousand of twenty years and upward, twenty-two thousand firstborn yields roughly one firstborn to forty-four males, which has been urged as a ground for rejecting the historical truth of the narrative altogether. His first answer is a general one: it is hard to conceive that a writer who produced so many complicated calculations would have inserted among them one fraught with such apparent improbability. His solutions are two. Either the firstborn here are restricted to those under twenty who had not been included in the census already taken — a limitation he thinks the destruction of the Egyptian firstborn also observed, since there appears to have been about one death to a house — or the term covers the firstborn of every household, including the children of concubines and slaves. With allowance made for the proportion of the sexes, for early deaths, and for counting only those firstborn on the father's side as well as the mother's, he reckons families of eight or nine children would account for the figure.

How the surplus was picked out is the most disputed detail, and here the witnesses are at open odds. Gill reports the rabbinic answer he finds in Jarchi and Abarbinel and in the Talmud, that it was settled by lot: twenty-two thousand slips written a Levite and two hundred and seventy-three written five shekels, mixed together and drawn. He mentions that some supposed the money was paid out of a public stock instead, which was a ready way of doing it, though whether reasonable is less clear, since the firstborn were the property of particular persons. Clarke reports the same lot and will not have it: he calls it a most stupid and silly tale, since no intelligent people could have settled the matter that way, and thinks it much more likely the charge was met from a general fund. Henry and Wesley take a third road, supposing the exchange began with the eldest of the firstborn and worked downward, so that the two hundred and seventy-three redeemed with money were the youngest.
44:
The shortfall has to be made good, and Calvin states the principle before the sum. Since the complete portion of God was not found in the tribe of Levi, it had to be supplied from elsewhere; the Levites, infants and men together, fell two hundred and seventy-three short of the firstborn, and God required five shekels of the sanctuary for every head. He adds the one thing the reader needs in order to know what was paid, that the shekel of the sanctuary was the double shekel, worth two of the ordinary kind. Gill converts it into his own currency at about eleven or twelve shillings a head, and notes that this became the settled price of such a redemption afterwards. Ellicott points to where the standard is first defined and observes that the law of redeeming the firstborn at five shekels came into operation from this moment.

Who actually paid is not stated, and Gill is candid about the gap. Children of a month old could not pay, so their parents paid for them; but of whom the money was exacted, and how the two hundred and seventy-three were identified, the text does not say. He runs through the possibilities once more without settling them. Ellicott is equally frank that the manner of determining the families is not recorded, and offers the two guesses that seem to him open — that the money was taken from those most recently born, since the standing law would from now on fall on each newly born firstborn, or that it was decided by lot.

The cattle are dealt with in a clause and raise a question of their own. Ellicott observes that there appears to have been no numbering of them at all; had there been, it would have supplied an argument about the scope of the original command, since the firstborn among cattle could not otherwise have been counted. What happened instead was wholesale — the whole of the Levites' cattle given in redemption of all the firstlings of all the other tribes. Wesley guards the transaction from a misreading: the cattle were not taken away from the Levites, nor sacrificed, any more than the Levites themselves were, but presented before the Lord by way of acknowledgment, the beasts remaining with the men as their support in God's work.

Ellicott then denies something the whole arrangement is usually taken to prove. The assertions frequently made about a priesthood of the firstborn being transferred to the Levites appear to him altogether without foundation, and he gives three reasons. The priesthood exercised in patriarchal times was not restricted to the firstborn but belonged to the head of every family. It was exercised before the exodus, and so before the command to sanctify the firstborn was ever given. And the priesthood, having belonged not to the firstborn exclusively but to Israelites at large, was thenceforth confined to the family of Aaron, who inherited it not as substitutes for the firstborn but in the place of the whole nation. Gill ends the chapter on the man who handled the money rather than the doctrine, noting that Moses did as he was commanded and did not convert any of it to his own use or to any use but the one appointed.
